query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Trace carbon doping in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys will improve their glass‐forming ability and enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state relative to otherwise identical alloys without carbon.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy (e.g., a Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 composition) synthesized by arc melting and rapid solidification under an inert atmosphere.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, minor concentration of carbon during alloy synthesis (e.g., adjusting carbon content within a narrow range such as 0.5–2 at%).
generation.conditions: Alloys should be prepared under identical inert atmosphere and controlled rapid cooling conditions (using arc melting and rapid solidification) so that the only variable is the carbon content; the effect is expected to be most measurable when cooling rates are high enough to capture differences in amorphization behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: Modification of the local atomic bonding environment where added carbon interacts with phosphorus, potentially hindering crystalline nucleation and promoting disordered short-range ordering in the amorphous phase.
generation.mechanism: By bonding strongly with phosphorus, carbon doping increases the local configurational entropy and disrupts the regular ordering required for crystallization. This disruption enhances the kinetic barrier to nucleation, thereby lowering the critical cooling rate for forming an amorphous structure and increasing the temperature at which crystallization initiates.
generation.predicted_outcome: The carbon-doped alloy will require a lower critical cooling rate for amorphization and will exhibit a higher onset temperature for crystallization in differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurements compared to the undoped baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy prepared under the identical processing conditions but without carbon doping.
generation.boundary: This positive effect is anticipated under rapid cooling conditions typical of arc melting and rapid solidification; if cooling rates are too slow or if the carbon content falls outside an optimal window (either too little or too high), the effect on glass-forming ability and thermal stability may not be observed.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal carbon concentration and the precise atomic-scale interactions remain uncertain, as do potential interactions with other alloying elements; systematic compositional studies are needed to refine these parameters and understand the limits of the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys with the same phosphorus-containing high-entropy base composition: one set with no additional carbon and another with a trace amount of carbon (targeted between 0.5 and 2 at%). Synthesize both sets using arc melting and rapid solidification in an inert atmosphere to ensure identical processing conditions. Characterize the samples using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to confirm the amorphous structure, and use differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the onset temperature of crystallization and the critical cooling rate needed to form the amorphous state.
measurements: Critical cooling rate for full amorphization
XRD peak profiles to assess amorphous versus crystalline content
TEM imaging for short-range order characterization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the carbon-doped alloys do not show a statistically significant improvement in glass-forming ability (i.e., no reduction in the critical cooling rate) or an increase in the crystallization onset temperature compared to the undoped alloy. Additionally, if the carbon dopant leads to enhanced crystallization or deleterious phase separation rather than an amorphous structure, the hypothesis would be refuted.

Furthermore, recent findings on NiNbP bulk metallic glasses highlight how phosphorus additions enhance glass-forming ability and increase hardness, albeit at the cost of some ductility []. Inspired by these results, this study explores the microstructure, mechanical behavior, and phase stability of phosphorus-containing alloys to better understand and utilize their unique properties. The combination of high configurational entropy and phosphorus enrichment in these alloys suggests their potential for applications in demanding environments that require enhanced wear resistance, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability. These properties position them as promising candidates for use in the aerospace, automotive, and tooling industries, as well as in advanced coating technologies and high-performance structural components.
